problem.title: Retail demand forecasting
problem.context: A retailer forecasts weekly demand per store and product: 400 stores and 30,000 products. Every Monday the forecasts for the next eight weeks feed the replenishment system, which orders stock. Sales from the tills reach the company's data warehouse every night; promotions and public holidays move demand strongly. A team of three data scientists owns the forecasting pipeline end to end. The data warehouse is run by the central IT department, which the team cannot change.

requirements.text: Produce, every week, the forecast per store and product for the next eight weeks, and deliver it to the replenishment system by Monday 06:00.
Run the forecast again for any past week exactly as it was produced.
Try new model ideas and compare them with the production model on past weeks before they replace it.
Asked for the forecast of a week up to two years back, the team produces the same numbers within one working day.
A new model idea that beats the production model on past weeks reaches production within one week, with no manual step except the approval.
When a weekly run fails, the team is told within 15 minutes, and the replenishment system never receives a partial forecast.
A new team member can run the whole pipeline on their own machine within their first week.
Three data scientists, with no data engineers; the data warehouse stays as it is.
The weekly run must fit in the six hours between the nightly load and the Monday deadline.

values: Execution: Managed workflow orchestrator with containerized Python jobs
Historical replay: Immutable input snapshots, code versions, and model artifacts
Model promotion: Automated evaluation and approval-gated champion switch
Forecast delivery: Write to staging, validate completeness, then atomically publish
points.description: A managed orchestrator runs containerized Python forecasting jobs against immutable input snapshots, recorded code versions, and model artifacts, enabling exact historical replay. Results are evaluated automatically; an approval gate selects the champion, which writes forecasts to staging, validates completeness, and atomically publishes them. Trade-off: This gains reproducibility, controlled promotion, and protection against partial or incomplete delivery. It gives up operational simplicity and may require extra storage and compute for immutable artifacts, while approval and validation add latency to releases.

values: Execution: Serverless scheduled batch functions
Historical replay: Versioned source snapshots and saved forecast outputs
Model promotion: Automated backtest with approval-gated deployment
Forecast delivery: Staging tables with completeness checks and atomic swap
points.description: Scheduled serverless batch functions generate forecasts from versioned source snapshots, preserving inputs and outputs for historical replay. Automated backtesting evaluates candidate models, while approval-gated deployment promotes them; forecasts are written to staging tables, checked for completeness, and published through an atomic swap. Trade-off: This gains reproducibility, controlled model changes, and consistent forecast delivery, but adds storage and operational coordination for snapshots, outputs, and staging, while approval gates can delay model updates.

values: Execution: Team-managed single VM running scheduled containers
Historical replay: Retain model versions and forecast outputs only
Model promotion: Manual notebook comparison and replacement
Forecast delivery: Direct write to replenishment table after run
points.description: A team-managed VM runs scheduled containers that generate forecasts, retaining model versions and forecast outputs for reference. The team manually compares models in notebooks, replaces the selected model, and each run writes its forecast directly to the replenishment table. Trade-off: This is operationally simple and retains enough history for basic comparison. It gives up automated promotion, richer replay context, and a delivery safeguard between forecasting and replenishment, so an erroneous run can propagate immediately.

values: Execution: Managed container batch with a lightweight scheduler
Historical replay: Immutable warehouse extracts and versioned code
Model promotion: Champion-challenger registry with approval
Forecast delivery: Versioned forecast tables with pointer swap
points.description: A lightweight scheduler runs forecasting jobs in managed containers, using immutable warehouse extracts and versioned code to reproduce historical runs. Approved champion or challenger models are promoted through a registry, and forecasts are published in versioned tables by switching the active pointer. Trade-off: This gains reproducibility, controlled model promotion, and clean forecast cutovers, but gives up low-latency delivery and incurs storage, registry, approval, and batch-operational overhead.

Trade-off: This provides reproducibility, controlled releases, and protection against incomplete deliveries, but requires additional storage and operational coordination. Approval gates and completeness checks can delay promotion or forecast availability, and managed scheduled runs may incur ongoing infrastructure cost.

Trade-off: This provides reproducibility, auditable promotion, and protection against partial or incomplete deliveries, but consumes storage and management effort for immutable artifacts and staging data. Approval gates and validation also add latency and operational coordination before forecasts reach consumers.

Trade-off: This provides reproducibility, auditable model promotion, and safe, rollback-friendly delivery, but batch execution and approval introduce latency and operational overhead, making rapid or real-time forecast updates less convenient.

values: Execution: Managed declarative workflow for containerized forecast stages

Trade-off: This gains reproducibility, controlled promotion, and consistent consumer-visible releases. It gives up some delivery speed and operational simplicity because replays, approvals, artifact management, and staged publication add coordination and infrastructure overhead.

adrs.title: Where should weekly forecast jobs run?
adrs.context: The pipeline must run every week within a six-hour window and remain manageable by three data scientists. A local path helps onboarding, while managed execution reduces infrastructure work; none of the candidate platforms has yet been benchmarked on the full workload.

options.name: Autoscaled managed orchestrator
values: Execution: Managed workflow orchestrator with autoscaled container jobs
pros: Managed scheduling and autoscaling reduce routine operations and provide capacity headroom.
cons: The complete workload still needs a measured six-hour run and a documented local setup.
options.reason: Choose this when capacity headroom and managed orchestration are the priority.

options.name: Scheduled managed containers
values: Execution: Managed container workflow with scheduled runs
pros: A simple scheduled container avoids a serverless duration ceiling and remains operationally small.
cons: Local execution and end-to-end runtime need acceptance checks.
options.reason: Choose this for a straightforward batch container workflow.

options.name: Lightweight managed batch
values: Execution: Managed container batch with a lightweight scheduler
pros: A lean scheduler and managed workers limit the team's infrastructure burden.
cons: Peak workload capacity and the six-hour objective need measurement.
options.reason: Choose this when a small batch control plane is preferred.

options.name: Declarative managed workflow
values: Execution: Managed declarative workflow for containerized forecast stages
pros: The declared stages can support both local runs and scheduled managed execution.
cons: The declarative workflow adds setup and still requires runtime evidence.
options.reason: Choose this when portability and repeatable stages matter most.

options.name: Team-managed VM
values: Execution: Team-managed single VM running scheduled containers
pros: A single host is conceptually easy to inspect and may be simple to run locally.
cons: It places operations on a small science team and does not resolve replay, automation, or publication safety.
options.reason: Dropped after the seed left several stressed requirements unresolved.

adrs.title: What must be retained for historical replay?
adrs.context: The team must reproduce a forecast from up to two years earlier within one working day. Retaining output numbers alone is insufficient to rerun the computation; the input data, code, and model state need to be tied to each run.

options.name: Immutable complete run record
values: Historical replay: Immutable input snapshots, code versions, and model artifacts
pros: Pins the source data, code, and model state needed to reconstruct the run.
cons: Requires storage lifecycle management and snapshot capture.
options.reason: Chosen by the managed workflow and container alternatives for complete replay provenance.

options.name: Immutable extract, code, and model artifacts
values: Historical replay: Immutable warehouse extracts, versioned code, and model artifacts
pros: Provides the input extract and executable model state required for reruns.
cons: The extract process and two-year retention need operational ownership.
options.reason: Chosen for the lightweight batch option because it creates an explicit run record.

options.name: Point-in-time extract with pinned commit and model
values: Historical replay: Point-in-time warehouse extracts, code commits, and model artifacts
pros: Ties each replay to point-in-time data, an exact source commit, and model state.
cons: Point-in-time extraction and retention add storage and pipeline complexity.
options.reason: Chosen for the declarative workflow's reproducible shared replay harness.

options.name: Versioned inputs and saved outputs
values: Historical replay: Versioned source snapshots and saved forecast outputs
pros: Preserves outputs that replenishment actually received.
cons: Does not ensure full immutable inputs and model artifacts for rerunning the calculation.
options.reason: Set aside after the seed showed that retained results alone leave replay incomplete.

options.name: Retain only models and forecasts
values: Historical replay: Retain model versions and forecast outputs only
pros: Uses less storage and preserves delivered values for inspection.
cons: Cannot reconstruct the source data and complete computation.
options.reason: Dropped because it misses exact historical rerun requirements.

values: Model promotion: Automated replay comparison with approval-gated registry promotion
pros: Reuses the replay harness to compare candidates and prepares a governed promotion.
cons: Harness upkeep and approval integration add workflow complexity.
options.reason: Chosen for the declarative approach to make comparisons part of the pipeline.

options.name: Manual notebook comparison
values: Model promotion: Manual notebook comparison and replacement
pros: Scientists can explore candidates with familiar tools.
cons: Manual comparison and replacement exceed the permitted manual approval step.
options.reason: Dropped because it does not meet the development velocity scenario.

adrs.title: How should forecasts become visible to replenishment?
adrs.context: The replenishment system must receive the weekly forecast by its deadline and must never see a partial result. A staging area with completeness validation and a single publication action creates a clear all-or-nothing boundary; the workflow also needs a separate failure alert within 15 minutes.

options.name: Staged partition atomic publish
values: Forecast delivery: Staged partitions with completeness checks and atomic publish
pros: Checks partition completeness before exposing the result and supports batch-scale delivery.
cons: Validation and the publication action must fit the deadline; alerts are a separate configuration.
options.reason: Chosen for the autoscaled orchestrator's partitioned output.

options.name: Staging table atomic swap
values: Forecast delivery: Staging tables with completeness checks and atomic swap
pros: Keeps incomplete writes out of the active table and gives replenishment one complete version.
cons: The destination's swap semantics and failure alerts must be verified.
options.reason: Chosen for the scheduled container alternative's simple consumer handoff.

options.name: Versioned tables with pointer swap
values: Forecast delivery: Versioned forecast tables with validated pointer swap
pros: Activates one validated forecast version and allows rollback by changing the pointer.
cons: The pointer update and consumer read behavior must be coordinated.
options.reason: Chosen for registry batch delivery with explicit versions.

options.name: Staged versioned atomic publication
values: Forecast delivery: Staged versioned outputs with atomic publication
pros: Preserves prior versions and makes each published forecast visible as one complete result.
cons: Staging and retention add storage, and failure alerts still need a monitored path.
options.reason: Chosen for the declarative workflow's versioned output boundary.

options.name: Direct replenishment write
values: Forecast delivery: Direct write to replenishment table after run
pros: Avoids a staging and publication layer.
cons: A failed run can leave partial data visible to replenishment.
options.reason: Dropped because it conflicts with the never-partial reliability requirement.
